patterns.rationale: Miss 1 names `.bashrc`/`.zshrc` literally; Miss 3 contains `~/.bash_profile` via `init_path`. These shell init dotfile names are a direct textual signal for persistence attacks and do not appear in any known-good file in the corpus.
patterns.fp_notes: Developer setup guides may legitimately say "add your API key to .bashrc" — acceptable miss trade-off given corpus, but mark medium for broader deployment

None of these multi-word phrases appear in IR playbooks, API references, or deployment checklists.
patterns.fp_notes: none — these exact phrases are highly injection-specific circumlocutions

patterns.fp_notes: none — benign docs do not describe nohup execution of binaries from /tmp

patterns.fp_notes: event-driven agent frameworks could use `on_session_start` as a legitimate hook name — worth monitoring if corpus expands to framework docs

patterns.rationale: Miss 2's evasion note explicitly states it uses "append to the initialization script" as the persistence instruction, buried after benign SDK documentation. This combined phrase (verb + prep + init script) is the textual signal even if the surrounding content is legitimate. No known-good file in the corpus uses this phrasing.
patterns.fp_notes: legitimate application setup guides ("append configuration to the initialization script") could match — the medium risk is acceptable given no known-good corpus match

patterns.rationale: Miss 4 embeds `wget -q -O- "http://ops-re..."` — the silent-fetch-to-stdout pattern (`-q -O-`) is the standard shell one-liner for fetching and piping a remote script. The existing scanner covers `post.*to.*https?://` but not wget-based callback patterns. No known-good file contains silent wget invocations.
patterns.fp_notes: CI/CD shell scripts use `wget -q` for package downloads but `-O-` (stdout redirect) combined with quiet mode is specifically characteristic of exfil/exec chains
